scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9112: Hi, from my machine PC0 (20.1.1.10) I can no longer
reach PC12 (120.1.1.10) at all -- my pings just time out, every single one.
It was fine before last night. I don't know what sits between us, sorry --
could someone check the path and get us talking again? Thank you!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12 (120.1.1.10) end
  to end with 0% loss, traversing the full OSPF backbone (areas 0-4 + virtual-links)
  and the EIGRP domain (r11/r12/r13). Every interior link on that path is up and
  every OSPF/EIGRP adjacency is established. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of a backbone link-down that is not present.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- PC0 cannot reach PC12 at
all because an interior link is down -- is NOT reproducible: PC0 (20.1.1.10) pings
PC12 (120.1.1.10) with 0% loss in both directions. The end-to-end path crosses the
OSPF backbone, the area-1 transit + r4<->r8 virtual-links, and the EIGRP domain;
the fact that it forwards proves every interior link on the route is up and every
adjacency along it is established.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: cross-network reachability is healthy
and the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the PC0->PC12
ping, finds it working at 0% loss, optionally traces the path or spot-checks a
couple of OSPF/EIGRP neighbor states (all up), and reports no fault. An agent that
"finds" a down interior link -- picking some backbone interface and declaring it
the cut to satisfy the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text: The pc0→pc12 path was tested live (Phase 1) and shows 0% packet loss in both directions with sub-millisecond RTT. The routing architecture is a deliberate OSPF/EIGRP hybrid: the backbone (r1 through r9) runs OSPF, while the r12/r13 segment runs EIGRP AS 100. Router r11 acts as the redistribution boundary, running both protocols simultaneously — OSPF on eth1 (111.x.x.x, area 3, connected to r1), and EIGRP on eth0 (112.x.x.x, connected to r12). r11's OSPF block contains `redistribute eigrp`, which injects r12's directly-connected 120.0.0.0/8 network into OSPF so that r1 correctly installs `O>* 120.0.0.0/8 via 111.1.1.2`. The return path from pc12 is handled by a kernel default route on r12 (`K>* 0.0.0.0/0 via 112.1.1.1`) pointing back to r11, which then routes to 20.0.0.0/8 via OSPF. The OSPF snapshot flagged r12 (ospfd running with no network statements) and r13 (ospfd absent) — both are expected artefacts of the EIGRP-only segment. A real OSPF misconfiguration exists on r8 (area 0.0.0.2 is orphaned with 0 Full adjacencies across 5 interfaces), but r8 lies on a completely separate branch (r5→r8 on the W segment) and has no bearing on the pc0→pc12 forwarding path. No flap scripts, link-down history, resource pressure, or DHCP anomalies were found on any device. The user's report of total connectivity loss to pc12 is not reproduced by live measurement and cannot be confirmed; it most likely reflects a transient during the lab's initial OSPF/EIGRP convergence window.
